title: The Relationship of Irritable Bowel Disease with Zonulin Protein A and Pyroptosis
content:
Background/Objectives: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a common disease that makes life difficult. There is evidence that the pathophysiology of IBS is multifaceted, including mucosal inflammation, visceral hypersensitivity, microbial dysbiosis, dietary factors, and alterations in intestinal permeability. In our study, we found that pyroptosis can be induced by inflammatory responses that may cause increased intestinal permeability and intestinal permeability, in which zonulin protein plays a role in IBS. The aim of the study is to determine whether these markers will be predictors for IBS or not. 
Methods: Those who applied to the Harran University Research and Application Hospital Internal Medicine and Gastroenterology outpatient clinics between 01 April 2018 and 01 July 2019 did not have alarm symptoms, did not have systemic diseases affecting bowel movements, did not use drugs that could affect bowel movements, were over 18 years old, did not have pregnancy status, and Forty-four patients and 44 healthy individuals who signed the voluntary consent form, underwent colonoscopy and were found to be normal, diagnosed with IBS according to the ROME-IV criteria, were included on a voluntary basis. IL-1β, Nlrp3, Gasdermin-D and Zonulin Protein-A levels were studied in the patients and their serum levels were measured according to the normal reference value range determined by our laboratory.
Results: When the patient and control groups were compared, a significant difference was found between the mean IL-1β levels. The mean IL-1β level was found to be statistically significantly higher in the patient group (p=0.000). The mean serum IL-1β levels were 154.81±53.35 pg/ml in the patient group and 111.51±29.96 pg/ml in the control group. When the patient and control groups were compared, a significant difference was found between the mean NLRP3 levels. The mean NLRP3 level was found to be statistically significantly higher in the patient group (p=0.000). The mean serum NLRP3 levels were 38.85±24 pg/ml in the patient group and 22.5±10.78 pg/ml in the control group. When the patient and control groups were compared, a significant difference was found between the mean Gasdermin-d levels. The mean Gasdermin-d level was found to be statistically significantly higher in the patient group (p=0.009). The mean serum Gasdermin-d levels were 225±0.609 ng/ml in the patient group and 0.8611±0.48 ng/ml in the control group. When the patient and control groups were compared, a significant difference was found between the mean Zonulin Protein-A levels. The mean Zonulin Protein-A level was found to be statistically significantly higher in the patient group (p=0.001). The mean serum Zonulin Protein-A levels were 4.30±1.90 pg/ml in the patient group and 3.015±1.67 pg/ml in the control group. 
Conclusion: In the etiopathogenesis of IBS, zonulin protein a and pyroptosis-related marker levels (Nlrp3, Il-1b, Gasdermin-D); The fact that it was detected significantly higher in patients with ibs compared to healthy controls supports our predictions that pyroptosis can be induced by inflammatory responses that may cause increased intestinal permeability and intestinal permeability, in which zonulin protein plays a role in ibs.
